title: VLIW & Static ILP
summary: The compiler-scheduled alternative to dynamic out-of-order execution — bundling independent operations at compile time instead of discovering them at runtime.

slides.markdown:
**VLIW (Very Long Instruction Word)** takes a completely different approach from superscalar/OoO: instead of hardware discovering independent instructions at runtime, the **compiler** identifies them ahead of time and packs several operations into one very long instruction word — one slot per functional unit, all issued together every cycle.

Where a superscalar core needs scheduling logic to find parallelism on the fly, a VLIW core just executes whatever the compiler already decided should run together — the hardware itself stays comparatively simple.

slides.sectionTitle: Moving the burden to the compiler
slides.markdown:
This is the defining trade-off of VLIW: **the scheduling burden moves from hardware to the compiler.** A superscalar/OoO core spends real silicon (reservation stations, reorder buffers, wakeup logic) figuring out what can run in parallel, every cycle, for every program it ever runs.

A VLIW compiler does that analysis **once**, at compile time, with the luxury of arbitrarily more time and a global view of the code — then bakes the schedule directly into the instruction encoding. The hardware trusts the compiler's bundle completely and never re-checks it at runtime.

![A VLIW instruction bundle with independent slots for an ALU, a load/store unit, and a branch unit, all issued together](assets/vliw-bundle.svg)

Each slot is dedicated to a specific functional unit — one always feeds the ALU, another the load/store unit, and so on. If the compiler can't find independent work for a slot that cycle, it fills it with a **no-op** — wasted bundle space is the visible cost of the compiler running out of parallelism.

assets.alt: A VLIW instruction bundle with independent slots for an ALU, a load/store unit, and a branch unit, all issued together

slides.markdown:
| | VLIW | Superscalar / OoO |
|---|---|---|
| Who schedules | Compiler, at compile time | Hardware, at runtime |
| Hardware complexity | Simple — no dynamic scheduling logic | Complex — reservation stations, ROB |
| Handles runtime surprises | Poorly — schedule is fixed | Well — reacts to actual latencies |
| Needs | A very smart, static-analysis-capable compiler | More silicon, power |

**How to decide:** VLIW wins when a compiler can accurately predict every operation's latency ahead of time; OoO wins when latencies are runtime-dependent and unpredictable.

slides.sectionTitle: Where VLIW struggles — and where it thrives
slides.markdown:
VLIW's fixed schedule assumes the compiler knows each operation's latency in advance. A **cache miss** breaks that: the compiler scheduled a dependent instruction assuming a 4-cycle load, but a miss makes it take 200 — a static schedule has no way to react mid-flight the way dynamic scheduling does.

It's tempting to call VLIW a failed idea — it isn't. It **thrives** wherever timing is predictable: DSPs, some ML accelerators, and embedded cores running tight, cache-miss-free loops, where the compiler's static schedule matches reality.

Take the same instructions used in superscalar-execution's trace, now on a 3-wide VLIW machine (1 ALU slot, 1 load/store slot, 1 branch slot per bundle):

```
I1: R1 = R2 + R3     ; ALU
I2: R4 = load [R5]   ; load/store
I3: R6 = R1 + R7     ; ALU, RAW on I1
I4: R8 = R4 + R9     ; ALU, RAW on I2 (load latency 3 cycles)
```

A VLIW compiler does this scheduling **once, at compile time**, using a fixed, known load latency (say 3 cycles) baked into the ISA contract. It packs Bundle 1 = `{I1, I2, nop}` — no runtime check needed, the compiler already knows I3 must wait. Bundle 2 and 3 are filled with instructions from *elsewhere* in the program (if the compiler found independent work), or `nop`s if it didn't. Bundle 4 = `{I3, nop, nop}` fires once I1's result is guaranteed ready. I4 can't be scheduled until 3 cycles after I2 issues, full stop — if the compiler mis-modeled the load latency (say a cache miss actually takes 40 cycles, not 3), **I4 reads garbage**, because there's no runtime check catching it the way a scoreboard or Tomasulo would.

slides.sectionTitle: Why VLIW needs the compiler to see everything
slides.markdown:
A VLIW core has essentially no runtime dependence-checking hardware — no reservation stations, no scoreboard, no dynamic scheduler — which is precisely what makes it cheap in area and power compared to an equivalent-width superscalar OoO core. But it means every piece of information an OoO core discovers dynamically must be known to the compiler **statically**, at compile time, before the program ever runs.

That includes exact functional-unit latencies (a fixed number of cycles for every operation, no variable-latency cache misses the schedule can't see coming), the complete dependence graph (which the compiler can only get right if it can prove pointers don't alias — see the pitfall slide), and branch outcomes it wants to schedule around (handled via **predication** — executing both sides of a branch and discarding one — or software pipelining across loop iterations, instead of hardware branch prediction).

This is the fundamental trade this topic keeps returning to: VLIW moves complexity from silicon (that runs on every cycle, for every instruction, forever) to the compiler (that runs once, offline) — a great trade when the compiler can actually deliver the analysis, and a bad one when it can't.

The single biggest reason VLIW struggles outside DSP/embedded niches: **pointer aliasing**. If a compiler cannot prove two pointers point to different memory (common in C with raw pointers, less common in languages with stronger aliasing rules), it must conservatively assume they *might* alias — and a VLIW compiler that gets this wrong doesn't just miss an optimization opportunity the way an OoO core would; it can schedule a load **before** a store that should have come first, producing a silently wrong answer with no hardware safety net to catch it.

```c
void scale(float *a, float *b, int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) a[i] = b[i] * 2.0f;  // does a alias b?
}
```
Without a guarantee that `a` and `b` don't overlap, the compiler must schedule every `a[i]` write conservatively relative to every `b[i]` read, forfeiting most of the parallelism VLIW exists to extract. This is exactly why VLIW thrives in DSP and media codecs — hand-annotated or restrict-qualified code with no aliasing — and struggles in general-purpose C/C++ workloads full of pointer-heavy, alias-ambiguous code, which is the concrete reason it lost the general-purpose CPU race to out-of-order superscalar designs despite being simpler silicon.

Despite losing the general-purpose CPU race, static VLIW-style scheduling is the dominant design in domains where the workload is known and regular ahead of time. **DSPs** (Texas Instruments C6000 family) and **VLIW-based GPUs/media processors** exploit exactly the property general-purpose code lacks: tight, hand-tuned or auto-vectorized inner loops (FFTs, FIR filters, video codecs) with statically provable, alias-free memory access patterns.

Intel's Itanium (IA-64) is the industry's cautionary tale in the other direction: it bet that compilers would get good enough at static scheduling, speculation, and predication to make VLIW-style (EPIC) designs competitive for general-purpose server workloads. Compiler technology never caught up to the bet, aliasing and irregular control flow ate the expected ILP gains in practice, and Itanium was discontinued after underperforming OoO x86 cores for most of its lifetime.

The lesson interview-relevant here: VLIW is not a worse idea than OoO in the abstract — it is a bet on the *compiler* instead of the *hardware* to solve scheduling, and that bet pays off exactly where the workload is analyzable and predictable, and fails where it is not.
